I did a quick scan of the article and it seems the problem doesn't lie with the testing, but how results are interpreted.(long read, lots of background on cases)

“The presence of a DNA profile says nothing about the time frame or the circumstances under which it came to be there,” says defense expert and researcher Dan Krane. “Test results can’t distinguish between the possibility of contamination, or evidence tampering, or, you know, murder.”

Basically if you don't have a good defense to poke holes in the theories of the prosecutor about how traces of your DNA ended up on a crime scene or victim, it could cost you dearly.

Useful article on how we should be critical about how we use DNA evidence and how we treat it in a court of law.

In other words - there's nothing scientifically wrong with DNA testing assuming that A) the evidence hasn't been tampered with intentionally, and B) it was properly collected in the first place. Then it's just a piece of evidence that may or may not be relevant depending upon the situation at hand... like all of the other evidence presented in court. The disparity in justice between those that can afford an amazing defense and those that can't has always existed. That's not the fault of DNA-based evidence.

Exactly, that's why I'd call the headline misleading.

It's the way we treat the evidence, DNA testing is always giving you an odd that it's a match(usually in the >99% range), when working with fragments the probability of it correctly matching starts to drop though the way it would be treated in court gives it more weight than it should as the general sentiment is that it is DNA evidence i.e. conclusive proof.

We can attribute (some) blame CSI and such for that feeling I guess.

Then again I could have missed other vital information so if people want to have an opinion they should read the article.

From similar machines that I've seen (not many, and I'm no expert) the big knob should be the stitch spacing 1- fine 4-coarse (this is probably metric so 1mm to 4mm) and the other one should be the type of stitch. Since the legend is missing you have to figure out what each one does by trial and error. 0 or 1 is probably the straight stitch.

Common problems that I've seen:

  • Needle facing the wrong direction. There is a little scallop near the hole of the needle. This must face the correct direction otherwise it will start breaking the thread. The correct direction is usually to the left but may vary.

  • Wrong tension: There is no tension adjustment for the bottom thread so the top thread must be tensioned to match the bottom. This tension varies by the thread and cloth being sewn and also by the air humidity cloud cover and the state of the stock market in Peru. Keep the tensioner clean and consult a wizard.
